answer.exemplar: Every lane named in the pilot list must also appear in the list of all proposed lanes, and the pilot list may name any number of those lanes, from none up to all of them. questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain what disjointness does and does not guarantee
questions.stem: A planner's memo keeps tram routes and bus routes on separate lists with no overlap. Explain what disjoint sets guarantee and what they do not guarantee.

answer.exemplar: Disjoint sets guarantee that no route appears on both lists, so their intersection is the empty set and their union simply combines the two lists. They do not guarantee that the two lists cover every route in the district, that the lists have the same size, or that one list is contained in the other. A route missing from both lists would be a third possibility the memo never mentions.

questions.explanation: Disjointness guarantees only that no route sits on both lists, so the intersection is empty. It says nothing about covering the district, matching sizes, or one list containing the other.
questions.hint: Separate what is ruled out from what is not.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain what an ordered pair records and why the order matters
questions.stem: A planner's memo records each signal timing as an ordered pair of a street and a time. Explain what the pair records and why swapping its entries matters.

answer.exemplar: The pair records one street together with one timing for that street, and the order says which entry belongs to which role, so (Oak Street, 7 a.m.) means the Oak Street signal at seven in the morning. Swapping the entries would put a time in the street slot and a street in the time slot, producing a different pair that no longer fits the memo's table.

questions.explanation: Each pair gives a first entry and a second entry, and the order assigns the roles. Swapping them breaks the record, so (Oak Street, 7 a.m.) and (7 a.m., Oak Street) are two different pairs.
questions.hint: Ask what each position in the pair holds.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Function written as a set of ordered pairs
questions.learningObjective: explain how to test a list of pairs for being a function
questions.stem: A planner's memo writes a set of ordered pairs that maps districts to funding levels. Explain how a reader can tell from the list alone that it is a function.

answer.exemplar: A reader can check that no first entry appears twice, because a function must send every input to exactly one output. If the district 4 appeared in two pairs, the set would give that district two different funding levels and would describe a relation rather than a function. Repeated second entries are acceptable, since two districts may receive the same funding level.

questions.explanation: Scan the first entries: if no input repeats, each one has exactly one output, which is the definition of a function. Repeated outputs are harmless, and repeated inputs are what break the rule.
questions.hint: Check the first entries for repeats.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain what one-to-one means and what it forbids
questions.stem: A planner's memo matches housing units to households, one unit to one household. Explain what one-to-one means here and what it would not allow.

answer.exemplar: One-to-one means every housing unit is matched with a different household and every household is matched with a different unit, so the two lists have the same length and no unit or household appears twice. It would not allow two households to share the same unit, a unit to be left without a household, or the two lists to be different lengths, and it says nothing about whether a match is a good one.

questions.explanation: One-to-one means every unit meets a different household and every household meets a different unit, so the lists match one for one. It forbids repeats and leftovers, and says nothing about the quality of a match.
questions.hint: Ask what a repeat would do to the pairing.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a converse differs from the original claim
questions.stem: A planner's memo argues this: if a street has a median, then the speed limit is 35. Explain how the converse of that claim differs from the original statement.

answer.exemplar: The original says a median forces a speed limit of 35, while its converse says a speed limit of 35 forces a median. The two statements are not the same and one does not follow from the other, because a street could have a limit of 35 for some other reason. The memo therefore needs separate evidence before it can treat the converse as true.

questions.explanation: The original runs from having a median to a limit of 35, and the converse runs from the limit back to the median. A street could have that limit for another reason, so the converse does not follow.
questions.hint: Compare the order of the two claims.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a contrapositive is built and why it means the same thing
questions.stem: A planner's memo reasons that if a street has a bike lane, then its speed limit is 30. Explain how the contrapositive of that claim is built and why it means the same thing.

answer.exemplar: The contrapositive is built by negating both parts of the claim and then reversing them, so it reads if the speed limit is not 30, then the street has no bike lane. It means the same thing because a claim and its contrapositive are true in exactly the same cases and false in exactly the same cases, which is why a planner can use either form to support an argument.

questions.explanation: Negate both parts and reverse their order to get if the limit is not 30 then there is no bike lane. A claim and its contrapositive share every truth value, so either form supports the same argument.
questions.hint: Negate both parts, then reverse their order.
